Connes

GeometryTrianglesCoordinates
Game: Move the three corners of a triangle and watch a dot that checks whether all three sides match.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Press Make equilateral to see the dot land on O, and use Show vector sums to see how the turns add up.
Look for the math

Turn two corners of a triangle by a third of a full turn, add the results to the third corner, and a dot tells you whether all three sides are equal. The live cut-the-knot page now embeds a GeoGebra version; the Wayback capture from 28 September 2006 embeds the original Java applet Connes whose drawing and options this port follows.

A turn that comes back to where it started

Identify the plane with complex numbers and let j be a rotation through 120° counterclockwise. Three such turns make a full turn, so j³ = 1 while j ≠ 1, and therefore

1 + j + j² = 0.

Here j² is the turn through 240°, the same as 120° the other way. The applet turns B by j and C by j² about the origin O.

The criterion on the page

For a triangle labelled counterclockwise, the page claims that ABC is equilateral if and only if

A + jB + j²C = 0.

The logic test confirms this in both directions: on 1,080 exact equilateral triangles of different sizes, positions and orientations, on their small perturbations, and on all 15,625 configurations of three corners on a five-by-five lattice around O. The orientation matters: if the corners are labelled the other way, the applet swaps the two turns and uses the conjugate identity, and the iff still holds. The page states the formula only for the positively oriented case, which is exactly what the test checks there.

Why one pair of sides is enough

Treat A − C and B − C as the two sides meeting at C. If the triangle is equilateral, B is one 60° turn from A around C; turning B − C by 120° in the opposite direction makes it point exactly along C − A. So

(A − C) + j(B − C) = 0,

which is A + jB − (1 + j)C = 0. Since 1 + j = −j², this is the same as A + jB + j²C = 0. The test checks this shortcut too: it holds for every generated equilateral triangle and fails for every near miss.

Reading the picture

B₁ is B turned 120° one way, C₁ is C turned 120° the other way. The parallelogram rule adds those two vectors at the green corner; adding the vector to A gives the red dot S. The criterion says the rotated pair sums to exactly −A, so S lands on O precisely for an equilateral triangle. The picture keeps the red dot, the segment from S to A and the two arcs even when the parallelogram is hidden, just as the applet does.

Make the triangle equilateral, then drag A a little. Watch how far S moves from O, and try turning the parallelogram on and off to see where the two rotated vectors meet.
